headline: Slack water at the Wicopesset boulders: tog nosing in, bass gone nocturnal
subhead: The current went quiet like we said it would, and the fish that love slack are moving into the rocks while the stripers slide into the dark.
body_markdown:
Poled out to the Wicopesset field Tuesday morning on a dead low, and the water lay flat enough to see crab scuttle off the tops of boulders eight, nine feet down. That's the tell. When you can watch a green crab work its way across a rock from the skiff without the current smearing your view, you know the flow's gone soft. We flagged this last week — said the neap tide coming in around the 21st would take the teeth out of the rip through here, and that's exactly what's happened. Fishers Island Sound runs on current. Take the current away and the whole personality of this water changes.

The blackfish don't mind it one bit. I've been picking through the boulder chains off Wicopesset and the western end of Fishers with green crabs and Asian crabs on a simple knocker rig, 1 to 2 ounces depending on how much drift I'm fighting, and getting steady work — tog to four and a half pounds, mostly on the last two hours of the incoming when there's just enough push to make the bait look alive without turning your line into a bow. These aren't the giants you'll see come October, but for late July they're solid, and they're eating with confidence because that slack water lets them sit tight to the rock without burning energy fighting current. Stonington Breakwater itself has been quieter than the outer boulder fields — too much boat traffic and not enough current sweep to stack bait against the riprap right now — but Ram Island's north side, in that 12 to 15 foot pocket, has given up a few nice ones too on the same crab presentation.

Striped bass have gone exactly where the middle of summer sends them — deep and nocturnal. Daytime, I'm marking fish on the meter suspended over 20 to 30 feet off Wamphassuc Point and along the Mystic River channel edges, but they're not eating in the heat of the day, not with the water sitting where it is. I fished the last two hours of light into full dark off Esker Point Thursday, drifting live eels on a fish-finder rig with just enough weight to hold bottom in the current seam where the river meets the Sound, and connected with three fish in the mid-20s to low-30s inch range before midnight. That's the program right now — first light and last light, or better yet full dark, working the seams where cooler water from the Mystic River pushes against the warmer Sound water. Don't bother blind-casting the flats at noon. You're wasting good bait.

Fluke have been a grind. There are shorts everywhere in the shallower grass flats around Little Narragansett Bay, but keeper-class fish want the deeper edges — the channel drop near the Mystic River mouth, 25 to 35 feet, on the stronger half of whatever tide we've got left. I've had better luck there with a white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a bucktail than with bait, working it slow along bottom on the last of the ebb when there's still enough water moving to make the tail kick without needing to horse it.

The story everybody wants to hear about is albies, and I get it — Fishers Island Sound has produced early false albacore in years past when the water sets up right. New London's reading in the high 60s, Kings Point over 70, and the classic push pattern says bonito and albies ought to be scouting the eastern Sound corridor and Block Island approaches within the next few days as that warm water works east. I haven't seen a single fin yet off the Race or around Wicopesset, and I'm not going to tell you I have. But I'll be running my 8-weight rigged and ready in the skiff starting this weekend, glassing the rips off Fishers Island's east end and Watch Hill Reef on the outgoing tide, because when they show here, they show fast and they show hungry, usually working bay anchovies right on the surface where you can see the nervous water before you see the fish.

Sea bass have stayed dependable through all this — the boulder structure off Fishers Island in 20 to 40 feet keeps giving up decent fish on squid strips and small jigs, and that's not changing anytime soon. It's the fallback when the tog get picky or the bass won't show.

Looking ahead, the tide cycle is already rebuilding — we're a few days off the neap now and I could feel more push in the water Thursday than I did Monday. By the weekend the Race and the western Sound approaches should have real current back in them, which tightens up the tog bite around the breakwater again and gets the bass moving with more purpose after dark. If I had one trip to make this week, I'd take the Sunday night high around Esker Point with eels, and I'd have the fly rod rigged in the skiff every single day just in case the first fin shows early. That's how it works out here — you don't chase albies, you just make sure you're ready when they arrive.
